newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Latam oil exports to rise 1mln bpd by end-98.
newsitem.headline: Latam oil exports to rise 1mln bpd by end-98.

text.p: Latin American oil production is expected to rise by more than one million barrels per day (bpd) between now and the end of next year, and almost all of this will be exported to world markets, industry analysts said on Monday.
Colombia will provide a large slug of the 550,000 bpd rise forecast for the rest of this year, while Brazil and Venezuela should take the lions' share of another 550,000 bpd jump by the end of 1998.

Sondra Scott, Latin America analyst for Cambridge Energy Research Analysts, said the vast majority would be exported because little new refining capacity is expected in that time. She expected the new supply to displace some U.S. imports from further afield, especially the North Sea and West Africa.

"In the short run, U.S. production is going up so you will see some of the long-haul crudes losing market share. But in the longer term, as U.S. requirements go up and production declines, all the incremental increase will go to Latin America rather than long-haul suppliers."
Traders said North Sea and Nigerian crudes were most vulnerable to displacement because they were sold on the spot markets, while Saudi supplies to the U.S. were protected by long- term contracts.

Oil from Colombia's new Cusiana-Cupiagua fields is expected to lift this country's output by 135,000 bpd to 861,000 bpd by the end of this year, according to figures from the Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA), a branch of the OECD.

Additional rises from the Cusiana-Cupiagua fields will be partly offset by declines in other areas and by the end of 1998, analysts Petroleum Finance Corp expect Colombia to be producing 940,000 bpd, 320,000 bpd above current levels.

In Brazil, three new floating production vessels on the Marlim field in July, September and December this year are expected to add 110,000 bpd to current production of 895,000 bpd, the IEA said in its latest Monthly Oil Report.
In 1998, the IEA expects Brazil to account for the second largest rise in non-OPEC supply (after the U.K.), with output reaching an average of 1.174 million bpd, 254,000 bpd over the previous year.
Petroleum Finance Corp was less bullish on Brazil, but still saw a 155,000 bpd increase from now to the end of 1998, hitting 1.033 million bpd by that time.

Venezuela was expected to lead the pack in 1998, with average crude and condensate production rising 400,000 bpd from 1997 to 3.650 million bpd in 1998, according to estimates by the state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela.
Natural gas liquids output is seen steady at just under 200,000 bpd.
Ecuador is one of the few countries expecting more distillation capacity during the next 18 months, with the main Esmeraldas refinery adding 20,000 bpd in September this year.

But this will be more than compensated by an 80,000 bpd increase in export capacity of the main SOTE pipeline expected by the end of next year. Some analysts, however, were reluctant to include this volume before the project has got underway.
Mexico was seen adding another 145,000 bpd oil production from now to the end of 1998, reaching 3.122 million bpd at that time, according to Petroleum Finance Corp.
Including NGLs, Cera expects Mexican output to jump by 120,000 bpd from 1997 to average 3.690 million bpd in 1998.
